newsitem.title: CHINA: China says no to debate on socialism vs capitalism.
newsitem.headline: China says no to debate on socialism vs capitalism.

text.p: China on Wednesday blamed diehard Marxists for rekindling a debate on whether it should take the socialist or capitalist road, saying getting rich was what really mattered.

"Years of leftism have made it difficult for us to shake off all at once our worries about 'socialism' versus 'capitalism'," the People's Daily said in a front-page commentary, part of a series in the run-up to a crucial Communist Party congress.
The party mouthpiece said it was unnecessary to debate whether China should have embraced such un-Marxist concepts as free markets, private enterprise and stock exchanges.

The newspaper said the debate should stop to make way for policies "in the interest of productivity, in the interest of boosting overall national strength and in the interest of improving the lives of the people".
"We must boost productivity... if we are to realise our dream of becoming rich and strong," it said.

Ultra-leftists have in recent months attacked the capitalist-style reforms of late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping and diplomats said commentaries in the party-run press marked a campaign to eliminate lingering criticism before the party congress in September or October.

The People's Daily lauded the economic achievements of Deng, who ingeniously dubbed his reforms as socialism with Chinese characteristics, thus enabling him to push through changes seen by orthodox Marxists as ideologically incorrect.
"If the debate had been protracted... would Shenzhen be a prosperous and developing new city towering aloft in south China that it is today?" the People's Daily said.
The southern boomtown of Shenzhen is the showcase of Deng's market-oriented reforms that scrapped Stalinist-style central planning and liberated people to get rich.
Diplomats said the commentary was part of a drive by party leaders to defend Deng's legacy and the legitimacy of his heir, Communist Party boss Jiang Zemin, at the forthcoming congress.
"It's partly related to the debate over Deng Xiaoping and his legacy, which obviously will be one of the background things at the congress," one Western diplomat said.
"It allows people to experiment and justifies different forms of economic ownership," the diplomat said.
On Tuesday, the People's Daily dusted off the rhetoric of its most liberal reform era of the mid-1980s, saying China was in need of bold experimentation.

Party reformers and hardliners have been jostling for position in the run-up to the five-yearly congress that will set the path of the world's most populous nation and elect leaders who will govern China into the 21st century.
Party leaders have been holding their annual summer gathering at the seaside resort of Beidaihe, where much of the groundwork for the congress is being done.
No role model existed in the world for China's path of development, the People's Daily said.
"There is no ready-made model in the world to choose from for China's development," it said. "There is no ready-made way of doing things that can be copied indiscriminately."
"Everything needs to be put into practice, probing and creating," the newspaper said, adding that past mistakes could be blamed on lack of a real understanding of socialism.

China has redefined socialism to justify its embrace of capitalist tools. Jiang, who will use the congress to set his own stamp on party politics, said last May that Marxist socialism was "not unalterable".
